Team Description (under 500 characters):

We are a four-person student team from Multan, Pakistan, combining software development, cybersecurity experience, and a love of astronomy. We are building a fast public web tool that turns SPHEREx sky data into a time-lapse for any coordinates, with adjustable field of view, image add/subtract, on-the-fly spectra, URL-based queries, and easy data updates, so anyone can spot moving objects and help make discoveries.
summary:
Blinkfield – Project Summary
Blinkfield is a public web tool built for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge.
It lets anyone enter a sky position (Right Ascension and Declination) and view aligned NASA SPHEREx infrared images as a short film. Moving objects such as brown dwarfs, comets, and nearby stars stand out clearly against fixed background stars.
What the tool does
Plays SPHEREx images like a short video (blink)
Stacks images to reduce noise
Creates difference images so only moving or changing objects remain
Generates a spectral scan across the six SPHEREx detectors
Overlays Gaia DR3 and AllWISE catalogue sources
Shows contamination flags (ghosts, streaks, blooms)
Allows users to choose field of view (4–20 arcmin)
Supports shareable links with coordinates in the URL
Test fields (as required by NASA)
Barnard’s Star
WISE 0855
Epsilon Indi B
RW Aurigae and R Draconis
Technical details
Built with React and TypeScript
Data from NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA)
Easy to update when new SPHEREx data releases become available
Can be deployed quickly on Vercel
Why it matters
SPHEREx maps the entire sky every six months in 102 infrared bands. There is far too much data for any one person to examine by hand. Blinkfield makes this data accessible so that students, researchers, and the public can help discover moving objects — continuing the same method that once led to the discovery of Pluto and many brown dwarfs and comets.
details:
1. What does it do?

Blinkfield is a public web tool that allows anyone to enter a sky position (Right Ascension and Declination) and view NASA SPHEREx infrared images of that area as a short film.

It helps users quickly notice objects that are moving or changing brightness — such as brown dwarfs, comets, asteroids, and nearby stars — by blinking, stacking, and differencing the images over time.

2. How does it work?

User enters sky coordinates (or opens a pre-loaded test field).

The tool searches the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) for SPHEREx images covering that position.

Images are grouped into time periods (epochs).

Small cutouts are downloaded and aligned onto a common north-up grid.

Background light (zodiacal light) is removed.

Users can:

Play the images like a video (blink)

Stack them to reduce noise

Create difference images (later minus earlier) so only movers remain

View a spectral scan across the six detectors

Turn on Gaia and AllWISE catalogue overlays

See contamination flags

3. Why was this project made? (Purpose & Benefits)

SPHEREx is mapping the entire sky every six months in 102 infrared bands and producing images of more than one billion objects. No single person can examine all this data by hand.

Benefits:

Makes complex NASA data easy for ordinary people to use

Helps students, teachers, and amateur astronomers take part in real scientific discovery

Speeds up the process of finding moving objects

Continues the successful citizen-science tradition (like Backyard Worlds and the discovery of Pluto)

Provides a simple visual way to explore time-domain infrared astronomy

4. What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact is to open SPHEREx data to the public so that more people can help discover new moving objects in the sky.

By turning difficult scientific data into a simple “blink and look” experience, Blinkfield aims to:

Increase public participation in astronomy

Support education and student projects

Help professional and amateur researchers quickly check interesting sky positions

Encourage future discoveries of brown dwarfs, comets, and other nearby objects

5. What tools, languages, hardware, or software were used?

Software & Languages:

React

TypeScript

Vite

Nitro (server)

Custom FITS image handling

TAN + SIP projection for accurate sky alignment

Data Sources:

NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) – SPHEREx data

Gaia DR3 catalogue

AllWISE catalogue

Deployment:

Vercel (web hosting)

Hardware:

No special hardware was required. The project runs entirely in a normal web browser.

6. How is your project creative?

Blinkfield is creative in several ways:

It turns complex multi-band infrared survey data into a simple, film-like experience that anyone can understand.

It combines blinking, stacking, differencing, spectral scanning, and catalogue overlays in one clean public tool.

It is designed to be easily updated when new SPHEREx data releases become available (only one line of code needs to change).

It follows the spirit of classic discovery methods (like the discovery of Pluto) but applies them to modern space-mission data in a user-friendly way.

The interface and features were carefully chosen so that both beginners and advanced users can get value from it.

7. What factors did you consider while developing the project?

We carefully considered the following factors:

Ease of use – Must be simple enough for students and the general public

Scientific accuracy – Proper image alignment, wavelength handling, and catalogue overlays

All official challenge requirements – Including test fields, spectral capability, field-of-view control, URL sharing, and contamination flags

Updateability – Easy to point the tool at new SPHEREx data releases

Performance – Fast loading of cutouts and smooth playback

Honesty – Clear limits (not official spectrophotometry, subtle motion, possible incomplete coverage)

Accessibility – Works in a normal browser without special software

Inspiration from past success – Tools like WiseView and the citizen-science approach that helped discover many brown dwarfs and comets
